patient.chief_complaint: Subtle cognitive decline over 6 weeks in well-compensated NASH cirrhosis patient
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. A. is a 58-year-old accountant with well-compensated NASH cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A, MELD 8), obstructive sleep apnea on CPAP, and type 2 diabetes, presenting at his wife's insistence for cognitive evaluation. She noticed 6 weeks of progressive forgetfulness, difficulty with sequential tasks at work (he made errors in spreadsheets he normally manages perfectly), increased irritability, and a reversal of sleep pattern (day drowsiness, nighttime wakefulness). He denies confusion, but psychometric testing reveals mild impairment. He has no jaundice, no ascites, no asterixis. His ammonia is 48 µmol/L — at the upper limit of normal (lab ULN 45 µmol/L). His CT head is essentially normal. His EEG shows subtle slowing. The key puzzle features: (1) well-compensated cirrhosis (MELD 8) — HE is unexpected at this stage; (2) ammonia at the borderline of normal; (3) NO asterixis; (4) CPAP non-adherence on review (SpO2 96%, and wife reports he frequently removes the CPAP mask overnight) — untreated obstructive sleep apnea causes cognitive decline AND worsens HE (hypoxemia impairs hepatic ammonia metabolism); (5) omeprazole use — PPIs increase ammonia by altering gut microbiome (PPI-related dysbiosis increases urease-producing bacteria); (6) metformin — safe in compensated cirrhosis but sometimes held causing glucose fluctuation. The diagnostic puzzle requires recognizing MULTIPLE subtle contributors to covert HE in a well-compensated patient who appears well.
